#Code for histogram
ggplot(data = college_grad_df,
       mapping = aes(x = median)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(
    x = "Median of earnings",
    y = "major categories",
    title = "Median earnings for each major cateogry"
  )

The shape of the distribution is a bell shaped curve slighlty off centre (to the left).

Exercise 2: Exploring relationship

#your code here
ggplot(data = college_grad_df,
       mapping = aes(x = sharewomen,
                     y = median)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Median earnings in majors with higher share of women",
    x = "Sharewomen",
    y = "Median earnings"
  )
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

The response variable is the median earnings and the explanatory variable is sharewomen. The trend seen on the graph implies that as the number of sharewomen increases the median earnings decrease.

Exercise 3: Fit and interpret a numerical predictor

#your code here
share_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ sharewomen,
      data = college_grad_df) 
share_fit %>%
tidy() 
## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
##   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)   56093.     1705.      32.9 1.27e-75
## 2 sharewomen   -30670.     2987.     -10.3 1.51e-19
share_fit_aug <- augment(share_fit$fit)

ggplot(share_fit_aug, mapping = aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted median",
    y = "Residules"
  )

median earnings = 56093.31 - 30669.94 x sharewomen
